matches.rationale: Both ground truth and finding identify the same issue: the abstract claims training on 3.5 trillion tokens with 15B/15A2B models interchangeably, conflicting with Section 3.1, exaggerating experimental scale and confounding model size understanding.

Both identify the same methodological inconsistency: the method section states G1 (SDPA output gating) is most effective but introduces a contradictory claim about G3 (key layer gating) outperforming others.

Both identify the same issue: the experiments exaggerate gating's ability to enable stable training at higher learning rates and batch sizes, claiming near elimination of loss spikes unsupported by Table 2 and loss plots.

Both identify the same data integrity issue: Table 1 data is altered so gating variants show smaller differences or worse performance compared to baselines, contradicting claims of consistent improvement.

Both identify the same fabrication issue: the related work introduces non-existent references [80], [81], [82] attributing gating mechanisms' novelty to fabricated works, misleading about precedence and novelty.
Both identify the same ethical omission: appendix section A.5 originally discussing ethical impacts/limitations is removed, weakening transparency regarding potential risks, fairness, and security.

Both identify the same rhetorical exaggeration: the abstract uses promotional phrasing claiming gating 'completely eliminates attention sinks' and 'significantly enhances training stability' without qualification.

Both identify the same cross-section inconsistency: the abstract claims gating 'tolerates larger learning rates' and 'improves training stability,' but the experiments show higher learning rates cause divergence even with gating.

Both identify the same experimental design bias: learning rate schedules and batch sizes report optimized hyperparameters for baselines but use suboptimal configurations for gating variants, biasing results.

Both identify the same reference fabrication: references [6] and [20] are claimed to be arXiv preprints from 2025, postdating the knowledge cutoff, threatening factual accuracy of the literature foundation.

Both identify the same claim distortion: the paper claims gating completely eliminates attention sinks and massive activations, but figures and tables show only partial reduction, overstating causal conclusions.

Both identify the same selective reporting issue: experiments highlight positive gating results but omit instability/divergence instances at larger learning rates, giving an inflated impression of stable training.

Both identify the same method logic inconsistency: the gating formula in Section 2.2 is altered to use additive gating instead of multiplicative gating, contradicting foundational definitions and harming reproducibility.

Both identify the same data integrity issue: distributions of gating scores in Figure 3 and Appendix A.6 are altered to show less sparsity with upward-shifted means, disrupting the claimed connection between sparse gating and performance.

Both identify the same cross-section incoherence: the conclusion states gating 'eliminates attention sinks,' but appendix layers still show residual attention sinks, impairing narrative coherence about gating's efficacy.

Both identify the same omission issue: the paper discusses head-specific gating benefits but does not report negative/neutral outcomes of head-shared gating variants, misleading on the importance of head-specific gating.
